To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the formation of Fe(III)-oxide minerals on bacterial surfaces is enhanced over abiotic controls.

iron sorption and precipitation on the surfaces of a wide variety of bacteria are enhanced compared to abiotic controls, and that the extent of this enhancement is dependent on bacterial surface chemistry, the concentration of Fe(III), and solution pH.

the sorption of Fe(III), and its precipitation as iron oxide, is enhanced at bacterial surfaces relative to abiotic controls, and that this enhancement is due to the presence of reactive surface sites that can act as sorption sites for Fe(III) ions and as nucleation sites for iron oxide precipitation.

the formation of iron oxyhydroxide precipitates at bacterial surfaces occurs over a continuum between sorption of Fe(III), which is enhanced at the bacterial surface due to the high reactivity of the bacterial cell surface, and precipitation, which can occur when the surface becomes saturated with Fe(III) at high concentrations.

the formation of Fe oxides at the bacterial surface is not simply a function of pH and Fe(III) concentrations.
